newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Were Nazi victims used for Austria anatomy book?.
newsitem.headline: Were Nazi victims used for Austria anatomy book?.

text.p: Vienna University said on Wednesday it had launched an inquiry into its celebrated "Pernkopf Atlas" of anatomical drawings to establish whether some of the subjects were victims of Nazi concentration camps.

Alfred Ebenbauer, rector of Vienna University, said the move was in response to approaches from Jewish groups in the United States and Israel who had sounded alarm bells over the drawings of limbs and shorn-headed corpses.
Some sketches in the "Atlas", which is still widely used around the world, bore swastikas and Nazi symbols alongside the artists' signatures.
"I am ashamed as a human being and representative of Vienna University at the university's shameful involvement in the horrors of National Socialism," Ebenbauer told reporters.
"I regret that in 50 years little has been done to shed light on to this dark chapter of Vienna University's history. The task is obviously more difficult at this late date," he continued.

He said the one-year inquiry would rely on letters, official files and statements from people alive at the time. It would extend beyond the "Pernkopf Atlas", named after its creator Eduard Pernkopf, to corpses and body parts stored at the university.

Investigators, led by Vienna University historian Gustav Spann, would examine documents and interview people who worked at the university between 1938 and 1945, during Nazi Germany's occupation of its smaller neighbour.
"There is little chance we will succeed in identifying all those pictured in the 'Atlas'. But we should at least be able to write that we have done everything possible," Spann said.
"We want to be able to add a word of explanation to new editions of the 'Atlas'," Ebenbauer added.

Pernkopf, a staunch National Socialist, was dean of Vienna University's medical faculty from 1938 and was university rector from 1943-1945. He delivered his acceptance speech in full Nazi regalia and died in 1955.
His "Atlas" is considered a bible of anatomy in Austria and has also won praise for the draughtsmanship of its artists.

Ebenbauer said he understood that it was normal practice at the time to use the corpses of criminals, among them people executed for political crimes, for anatomical drawings but he did not rule out that Jews had also served as subjects.
Austria's Jewish community and representatives of the nation's wartime resistance movement welcomed the inquiry.
"For us the religious element is the most important," said Paul Grosz, president of Vienna's Jewish culture organisation.
